cues: Thrivers. The surprising reasons why some kids struggle, and others shine.
A book by educational psychologist Michele Borba, published in twenty twenty-one.

data.title: Thrivers
data.subtitle: The Surprising Reasons Why Some Kids Struggle and Others Shine
data.author: Michele Borba, Ed.D.

cues: Here is the central idea. Intelligence, excellent grades, and impressive achievements, on their own, are not enough to prepare children for life.
Many parents today are raising Strivers instead of Thrivers: kids who perform brilliantly on paper, but struggle emotionally, socially, and psychologically when adversity hits.
Borba argues that resilience, happiness, and lasting success rest on seven character strengths, and every one of them can be taught.
The goal isn't just successful children. It's capable, independent, compassionate, and resilient human beings.

lines.html: Grades alone don't prepare kids for life.
7 character strengths — all of them teachable.

cues: Strivers seek outside validation. They measure success in grades, rankings, and awards. They fear failure, lean heavily on their parents, compare themselves constantly, and are vulnerable to stress and burnout.

Thrivers are different. They're driven from within. They know their strengths and weaknesses, see failure as a way to learn, manage their emotions, build meaningful relationships, and pursue success with purpose.
The difference isn't intelligence, talent, or family income. It's the inner resources a child builds over time.

data.footer: Not intelligence. Not talent. Not income. Inner resources.

cues: Borba organizes these seven strengths into three dimensions.
Nurturing the Heart: self-confidence and empathy.
Developing the Mind: self-control, integrity, and curiosity.
And cultivating the Will: perseverance and optimism.
Strength one: Self-Confidence. The ability to understand, appreciate, and trust your own capabilities.
It's built on three abilities: self-awareness, strength awareness, and finding purpose.
Help kids discover and nurture their natural talents. Avoid comparing them with others. Let them make independent decisions, and see who they are beyond their report card.
The lesson: help children become who they are, not who we want them to be.

data.name: Self-Confidence
data.def: Understanding, appreciating and trusting one's own capabilities.
data.lesson: Help children become who they are — not who we want them to become.

cues: Strength two: Empathy. Understanding another person's feelings, perspectives, and needs.
Its three abilities are emotional literacy, perspective taking, and empathic concern.
Talk about emotions openly. Encourage acts of kindness, consider different points of view, and create real chances to help others.
Success isn't only personal achievement. It's also making other people's lives better.

data.name: Empathy
data.def: Understanding another person's feelings, perspectives and needs.
data.lesson: Success also means contributing positively to other people's lives.

cues: Strength three: Self-Control. Regulating emotions, managing impulses, staying focused, and making responsible choices.
It depends on attentive focus, self-management, and healthy decision making.
Teach emotional regulation and delayed gratification. Cut unnecessary digital distractions, practice breathing and relaxation, and keep routines consistent.
Children must learn to manage their emotions, instead of letting emotions run their behavior.

data.name: Self-Control
data.def: Regulating emotions, managing impulses, focusing and deciding responsibly.
data.lesson: Manage emotions — don't let emotions dictate behavior.

cues: Strength four: Integrity. Acting on ethical principles consistently, even when nobody is watching.
Its building blocks are moral awareness, moral identity, and ethical thinking.
Set clear family values. Model honesty yourself. Discuss ethical dilemmas, encourage accountability for mistakes, and celebrate moral courage.
Character shows up in decisions and actions, not just words or intentions.

data.name: Integrity
data.def: Acting on ethical principles consistently — even when nobody is watching.
data.lesson: Character lives in decisions and actions, not words or intentions.

cues: Strength five: Curiosity. The willingness to explore, question, experiment, and discover new solutions.
It grows from a curious mindset, creative problem solving, and divergent thinking.
Welcome questions. Make time for unstructured play and experimentation. Resist giving answers right away, and support interests beyond school subjects.
Education should create kids who love learning, not just kids who are good at taking exams.

data.name: Curiosity
data.def: The willingness to explore, question, experiment and discover.
data.lesson: Raise kids who love learning — not just kids who ace exams.

cues: Strength six: Perseverance. The determination to keep pursuing meaningful goals, despite setbacks and failures.
It rests on a growth mindset, goal setting, and learning from failure.
Praise effort, strategy, and progress. Break big goals into small steps. Let children face manageable difficulties, step back from rescuing, and talk through lessons from mistakes.
Failure is not a permanent identity. It's a chance to improve.

data.name: Perseverance
data.def: Determination to pursue meaningful goals despite setbacks and failure.
data.lesson: Failure is not a permanent identity — it's a chance to improve.

cues: Strength seven: Optimism. Keeping a realistic sense of hope, and seeing possibilities even in hard times.
Its abilities are optimistic thinking, assertive communication, and hope.
Build a gratitude habit. Challenge overly negative thinking. Focus on what's within your control, encourage kids to voice their needs, and model constructive responses to adversity.
Optimism isn't ignoring reality. It's believing that constructive action is still possible.

data.name: Optimism
data.def: A realistic sense of hope — seeing possibilities in hard times.
data.lesson: Optimism believes constructive action is still possible.

cues: One of the book's most powerful ideas is the Multiplier Effect. Strengths grow stronger when they work together.
Self-confidence plus curiosity creates creativity and a stronger identity.
Self-control plus perseverance builds discipline and achievement.
Empathy plus curiosity deepens understanding and relationships.
Integrity plus self-control helps kids resist temptation.
Optimism, perseverance, and curiosity together fuel resilience, motivation, and deeper learning.
And integrity, curiosity, and empathy lead to meaningful purpose and social contribution.
Thrivers navigate challenges by drawing on several strengths at once.

data.footer: Thrivers draw on several strengths at once.

cues: The book draws on decades of research: Emmy Werner on resilience, Carol Dweck on growth mindset, Angela Duckworth on grit, Martin Seligman on optimism, Benjamin Bloom on talent, and Daniel Goleman on attention and emotional intelligence.
A key finding: resilient children often share two protective factors.
First, a meaningful relationship with at least one supportive adult.
Second, learned personal capabilities that help them navigate adversity.
Hard beginnings don't have to decide a child's future. Still, these strengths are protective factors, not guarantees, and not a substitute for professional mental health support.

data.caveat: Protective factors — not guarantees, and no substitute for professional mental health support.

cues: Borba also challenges some common parenting habits.
Over-emphasizing academic performance. Over-scheduling. Helicopter parenting. Constant comparison.
Relying too much on rewards. Solving every problem for kids. Neglecting emotional and moral growth. And imposing our own ambitions.
Too much protection can quietly take away the very chances children need to become independent, competent, and resilient.

data.footer: Over-protection removes the very chances kids need to grow independent, competent & resilient.

cues: So, how do you start? With simple everyday habits.
Daily: have real conversations without screens, ask about feelings, recognize effort and kindness, let kids solve problems, and practice gratitude together.
Weekly: support their genuine interests, talk about challenges and lessons, help others together, and spend time with no performance expectations.
Monthly: choose one character ability, practice it as a family, watch for growth, and gradually step back as children become more independent.
The book even includes a thirty-five question assessment to help identify your child's strengths.
Here are questions every parent should reflect on.
Does my child feel loved regardless of grades?
Am I developing my child's potential, or chasing my own ambitions?
Can my child solve problems without me?
Does my child know how to respond to failure?
Is there enough time to explore, play, and simply enjoy childhood?
Do I value kindness and integrity as much as achievement?
And am I modeling the strengths I expect to see?

cues: A critical perspective. The book's greatest strength is how it turns psychological research into practical, accessible strategies.
But much of it is rooted in the American educational context, so its ideas should be adapted to each family's culture, circumstances, and child.
It's best seen as a practical synthesis of research, not a universally proven formula for success.

pro.title: Strength
pro.text: Research turned into practical, accessible strategies — a clear framework beyond academic metrics.

con.title: Limitation
con.text: Rooted in an American context — adapt to your culture, circumstances and child.

data.verdict: A practical synthesis of research — not a universal formula.

cues: Academic achievement still matters. But it should complement character, not replace it.
We can't remove every difficulty our children will face. We can equip them to navigate those difficulties on their own.
The true measure of parenting is who our children become when we are no longer there to guide them.
Prepare the child for the road, not the road for the child.
Raise a Thriver, not merely a Striver.
